1.blurb: Persian Empire closes its long story with the same conquest told from the Sasanian side — al-Qadisiyyah and Nahavand, the commander Rostam Farrokhzad, and the death of Yazdegerd III. Where that book ends, this one begins.

Tang, Song & Sui China tells the story of the great Chinese empire at the far end of the Silk Road, the superpower whose court the fugitive Sasanian prince Peroz reached, and which never sent the army he begged for.

Islamic Golden Age opens with the Abbasid Revolution from the caliphate's side — Abu Muslim's clandestine network at Merv, the black banners, and the new dynasty that shifted Islam's center east toward Persia.

2.blurb: Islamic Golden Age devotes a whole chapter to the House of Wisdom and the translation movement in Baghdad, the lavishly funded effort that gathered Greek, Indian, and Persian learning into Arabic.
Islamic Golden Age covers the same Barmakid family from the caliphate's-eye view — the Buddhist-Persian converts from Balkh who ran the Abbasid state for three generations under Harun al-Rashid.

3.blurb: Islamic Golden Age tracks the same silver flood from the trade-network end — the millions of Samanid dirhams that ran up the Volga into the hoards of the north, and what happened when the Central Asian mines ran dry.
Delhi Sultanate picks up where the Ghaznavids' raids left off — the Turko-Afghan rulers who carried the Persianate court model deep into India, where it would shape the subcontinent for centuries.

4.blurb: Islamic Golden Age covers the Buyid seizure of Baghdad in 945 from the caliphate's side, with the amir al-umara title and the hollowing-out of the Abbasid caliph into a religious figurehead.

5.blurb: Islamic Golden Age tells the Seljuk arrival from Baghdad's side — Tughril Beg invited into the city in 1055, the expulsion of the Buyids, and the new sultan-and-caliph bargain.
Byzantine Empire narrates Manzikert from the losing side — the 1071 catastrophe that shattered the Byzantine field army, opened Anatolia to Turkish settlement, and set the empire on its long decline.

Scientific Revolution covers the European reform of the calendar five centuries after Omar Khayyam's — the Gregorian system Catholic Europe adopted in 1582, which the Jalali calendar had already bettered for accuracy.

6.blurb: Islamic Golden Age covers the Fatimids among the three rival caliphates — the Shia dynasty ruling from Egypt whose missionary network spread Ismaili belief east into Seljuk Persia, where Hasan-i Sabbah trained.
Mongol Empire tells the fall of Alamut from the conquerors' side — Hulagu's army taking the eagle's nest no one had ever stormed, burning its library, and al-Tusi's switch into Mongol service.

7.blurb: Al-Andalus follows the philosophical culture of Islamic Spain that produced Averroes, whose Incoherence of the Incoherence answered al-Ghazali a century later and shaped Latin Europe's reading of Aristotle.
Islamic Golden Age covers al-Ghazali's crisis, the Ihya, and the Incoherence of the Philosophers in fuller depth, including the live scholarly debate over whether his blow checked Islamic science.

8.blurb: Mongol Empire narrates the Otrar massacre and the Khwarazmian invasion from the Mongol side — the killed envoys, Genghis Khan's cold turn west, and the storm about to break on Persia.

9.blurb: Mongol Empire tells the 1258 sack of Baghdad from the conquerors' side — the trampled caliph, the burned libraries, the realistic casualty estimates, and the end of a five-century institution.
Mongol Empire covers Ayn Jalut in detail — the Egyptian Mamluks' 1260 victory in Palestine, helped by Hulagu's withdrawal on the Great Khan's death, the first real check on Mongol expansion.

10.blurb: Mongol Empire covers the Ilkhanate among the four khanates — Ghazan's conversion to Islam, Rashid al-Din's Compendium of Chronicles, and the Persianization of Hulagu's heirs.

Yuan Dynasty tells the story of Mongol-ruled China at the eastern end of the road the Pax Mongolica opened — the source of the dragons, phoenixes, and cloud-bands that flooded into Persian miniature painting.
Mongol Empire follows al-Tusi from the Assassin fortresses into Hulagu's service and the Tusi couple that would echo in Copernicus — the science the conqueror paid for after burning Baghdad.

11.blurb: Timurid Empire is the full story of the conqueror this chapter compresses — Tamerlane's rise in Transoxiana, the Genghisid-puppet legitimacy device, the towers of skulls, and the dazzling Samarkand he built from plunder.

Ottoman Empire covers the catastrophe of Ankara from the Ottoman side — Sultan Bayezid I's capture by Timur in 1402, his death in captivity, and the decade of civil war that nearly destroyed the young empire.

Timurid Empire devotes a chapter to Ulugh Beg the astronomer-king — the Samarkand observatory, the Zij-i-Sultani star catalogue, and al-Kashi's mathematics, the science crowning the Timurid renaissance.

Renaissance Italy tells the story of the other great late-medieval flowering happening at the same moment — Florence at its height while Herat reached its own, the two renaissances unaware of each other.

12.blurb: Safavid Persia opens with the same Ardabil order — Safi al-Din, the slow drift from quietist Sufism to militant Shiism, and the Qizilbash following that this chapter introduces and that book carries forward.
Safavid Persia picks up exactly where this book ends — the fourteen-year-old Ismail crowned at Tabriz after Sharur, and the violent imposition of Twelver Shiism that would define Iran ever after.
Persian Empire opens with the Achaemenid origin of the very title Ismail reached for — Shah, the king-of-kings word the Persians had used two thousand years before, kept alive through every conquest.
